name: Gareth Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley Pryce, a fifteen-person firm in a market town. Most of my clients are farms, plus builders, a garage and a couple of pubs. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, and in spring I'm out at farms with a laptop at the kitchen table going through the year's invoices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the farm visits, the cup of tea and the dog under the table, and knowing the family have done well or badly by the numbers I put together. What wears me out is the government changing the filing rules every couple of years so everyone needs new software. I've never used any of the AI tools and I don't intend to, if I can help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Accounting is about knowing your clients and knowing the rules, and no chatbot knows a sheep farmer's business like I do. I don't post online, but I'd say it in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's what I expected and it suits me. I'm paid well, I've got savings, and my fiancée Rhian and I are getting married next summer. If AI turns out to be hype, my biggest problem is the seating plan for my wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am at Hartley Pryce and keep my farm clients happy. Rhian and I would go ahead with the wedding and start looking for a house in the town. I'd keep putting money aside as I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at work that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farms are under pressure, with feed and fuel prices up, and a couple of my older clients might sell up in the next few years. That means fewer clients for the firm. But there are always new ones, and builders are doing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rhian do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She works in her father's building firm, doing the office and the orders. It's a good family business, three generations now. Her dad says there'll always be work for a man who's not afraid of a shovel.

say: Accounting is about **knowing your clients** and the rules.
No chatbot understands a **sheep farmer's business** like I do.
think: It's **what I expected**, and it suits me fine.
My biggest problem is the **wedding** next summer, not my job.
do: Carry on at **Hartley Pryce** looking after farm clients.
Go ahead with the **wedding** and start house hunting in town.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, my biggest problem is the seating plan for my wedding.
fieldNote: Gareth feels **secure** in his job, savings and family plans.
His existing worry is **farm clients** selling up under feed and fuel costs.
His trust in **family business** and hard work runs through everything he says.

steps.text: Keep visiting farm clients for spring year-end accounts
Marry Rhian next summer and look for a house in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we shouldn't rush into it, and that clients trust us because we're people. To friends I'd say it's the big firms in the cities that'll go all in, not us. I'd say the government shouldn't force it on small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. The checking and the returns are exactly what the card says the AI takes, and I don't know the tools at all. A younger accountant who uses AI could do my farm clients' accounts in half the time, and the partners at Hartley Pryce would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the partners decide, because I'm not going to learn something until I have to. I'd stop the house hunt for six months and put the money aside instead. If they bring in the tools, I'd learn them, grudgingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd keep it to myself, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say small firms will be fine, and also that a younger accountant could replace you. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm will be fine. Whether I'm fine is another question. I'd keep the first one for the pub and the second one for home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rhian say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say her dad would always have a place for me. And I'd say I didn't do five years of exams to be the office lad at a building firm. Then I'd probably come round to it.

The government shouldn't **force it** on small firms like ours.
The **big city firms** will go all in on AI, not us.
think: The checking and returns are **exactly what AI takes**.
A younger accountant using AI would be **twice as fast** as me.
do: Wait for the **partners' decision** before learning anything new.
Pause the **house hunt** for six months and save the money.
Learn the tools **grudgingly** if the firm brings them in.
S1.quote: A younger accountant who uses AI could do my farm clients' accounts in half the time, and the partners at Hartley Pryce would notice.
fieldNote: Gareth's work is **high-exposure** and he knows he's behind on tools.
He keeps a **public line** for the pub and a private worry for home.
His **pride** in his qualifications makes the family firm a hard fallback to accept.

steps.text: Wait for the Hartley Pryce partners to decide on AI tools
Pause the house hunt with Rhian for six months
Attend the firm's AI training only if it's required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's been pushed on us by tech companies who don't care what it breaks. At the pub I'd say the government let it happen. I wouldn't want handouts, though, I'd want work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone within a couple of years. Accounts are all desk work, so there's no waiting for the robots. I spent five years passing exams for a job that a computer will do better by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the wedding back to family and close friends and save about £15,000. I'd talk to Rhian's dad about joining the building firm, doing the books and learning a trade on site, because building is hands-on and has a few more years. I'd hold the savings and not buy a house until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and angry underneath it. It feels like the ground's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rhian's dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him if he'd take me on properly, not as charity, but as someone who does the books and learns bricklaying. He'd say yes, I think. It's not where I thought I'd be at 28.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mainly, for racing ahead without a thought. And the government for waving them through. It's not the farmers' fault or mine.

say: **Tech companies** pushed this on us without caring what it breaks.
think: My job's **gone** within a couple of years, because accounts are desk work.
Five years of **exams** were for a job a computer will do better.
do: Cut the wedding to **close family** and save about £15,000.
Join **Rhian's dad's building firm**, doing the books and learning a trade.
Hold off on **buying a house** until things are clearer.
S2.quote: I spent five years passing exams for a job that a computer will do better by 2028.
fieldNote: Gareth expects to **lose his job** fast and has no appetite for AI.
His fallback is **family**: his future father-in-law's hands-on building firm.
He blames **tech firms** and government, and rejects handouts in favour of work.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to close family and friends
Join Rhian's father's building firm and learn bricklaying
Ask Rhian's father for a proper place in the family firm
Keep the £15,000 wedding saving and delay buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and young people should be told now to learn a trade. I'd tell the lads at the rugby club to think hard before going to university. I'd still say I won't touch the AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end as the fast one, just slower. I'd be 32 in 2031. With five years, I could get a trade qualification before the AI takes my desk and still have years before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hartley Pryce and save hard, about £800 a month. In year two I'd start an evening bricklaying course at the college. We'd have the full wedding, but buy a smaller house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but more in control. It's a slower squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave accounting for a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the alternative is sitting at home, yes. My grandad was a stonemason. There's no shame in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the farm clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be using the AI themselves by then, probably through the bank. I'd still pop in if they asked me to, as a friend.

Think hard before **university**, and I still won't touch the AI myself.
think: It's the **same end** as the fast one, just slower.
Five years gives time for a **trade qualification** before the desk work goes.
do: Save about **£800 a month** while still at Hartley Pryce.

S3.quote: With five years, I could get a trade qualification before the AI takes my desk and still have years before the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Gareth uses the extra time to move toward **hands-on work**, which lasts three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change, so no need to panic. At work I'd say let's keep serving clients properly. I'd tell Rhian we've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd believe that farmers will still want a man at the kitchen table for a good while. Like I said with the slower one, I'd plan a trade, but not yet. Ten years is long enough for me to get married, buy a house and have a family before AI takes my accounting job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartley Pryce and aim for manager. We'd buy a house next year and have our first child within three years. I'd start a trade course maybe in year five, if things were clearly heading that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back of my mind. Mostly I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the partners keep you if you never learned the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for ten years, if I'm honest. I might have to learn the basics. I'd rather do that than lose the farm clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade first, then study if they want to. Something with their hands that a machine can't do quickly.

There's time to marry, buy a house and start a **family** first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. There'd be no time to learn a trade properly, and I'd be leaning on family. What would help is cheap apprenticeships for adults, so a man of 28 can learn bricklaying without starting on a teenager's wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Losing an accounting job isn't just money, it's telling your father-in-law you need his help. I'd do it, but it'd hurt.

headlineQuote: Losing an accounting job isn't just money, it's telling your father-in-law you need his help.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old accountant** at a market-town firm, mostly serving farms.
He's engaged to Rhian, whose father runs a **building firm**, and has good savings.
He's **calm** if AI stalls, but expects his desk job to go under AGI.
His fallback is **hands-on work**: bricklaying in the family firm, like his stonemason grandfather.
He blames **tech companies** and government, and wants apprenticeships rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn a trade properly.
whatWouldHelp: Affordable **adult apprenticeships** that don't start on a teenager's wage.
